summary:
Criminalising law in South Korea applies almost entirely to the military. Consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, but Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment. The Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023. Enforcement has been punitive and targeted: in 2017 the military ran what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

A trans soldier's case marks the sharpest documented harm. Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is documented as a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot flagged from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 chapter on South Korea covers events of 2024, including the December 2024 martial-law crisis and questions of assembly freedom, against a background the organisation characterises as relatively positive for media and civil society. Political turbulence of that order has affected the environment in which LGBT organising and protest take place.

Organised conservative opposition is a persistent factor: Christian protest groups have turned Pride events violent in Incheon and Busan, and opposition to a nondiscrimination bill has been sustained enough that activists cited its absence when describing their sense of personal risk. A gay travel guide assessing South Korea for visitors in July 2026 judged the country broadly positive for stays in Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods while flagging the military-law criminalisation, organised opposition and the absence of a national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

The trajectory on legal gender recognition is upward and fast: judicial guidance requiring surgical intervention, singleness and childlessness dated from 2011, was displaced in stages by the 2022 Supreme Court ruling on trans parents and the 2024 lower-court ruling rejecting a surgery mandate. Persons arriving from jurisdictions where recognition is unconditional may find the process still conditional on hormone therapy records and on marital status.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition no longer face a statutory surgery requirement following the 8 May 2024 ruling, which held for five plaintiffs on long-term hormone therapy that mandating surgery violates physical integrity. Marital status remains a gate: the Supreme Court's 24 November 2022 en banc decision allows recognition for transgender people with minor children only where they are not married.

Transgender South Koreans are excluded from military service. Those who do serve face article 92-6, under which consensual same-sex conduct is punishable by up to two years' imprisonment; the 2017 military investigation charged 32 personnel and produced a six-month prison sentence. The state's handling of Byun Hui-su's case, from compulsory discharge in 2020 through posthumous reinstatement in October 2021 and line-of-duty recognition in March 2024, is the reference point for how the defence establishment has treated a trans service member.

Everyday discrimination is documented at scale rather than anecdotal: 54% of LGBTQ youths reported classmate harassment in a 2014 finding, 51.5% of transgender adults reported harsh discrimination within a year in a 2018 study, and the 2025 nationwide survey of 585 transgender and non-binary young adults recorded stigmatisation at school, work and in transition-related care. Outed individuals face conversion-therapy recommendations, reported by 16.1%, with documented psychological harm. Public-health contact tracing has exposed identities, as in the May 2020 Itaewon cluster.

Institutional support remains thin. The Ministry of Health and Welfare declined in late 2023 to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, drawing public criticism from the National Human Rights Commission of Korea. LGBTI organisations may register, but registration has required litigation. Trans teenagers manage restroom access by avoidance, leaving school early or holding it in, with no legal mandate requiring schools to accommodate them.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory describes how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system. There is no stated birth-sex versus identity placement rule, no account of special units, and no documentation of solitary or segregation practice for trans detainees. Any placement question in that setting is unresolved here and would need prison-service regulations or oversight-body reports.

A Library of Congress global legal monitor entry on a South Korean Supreme Court decision permitting a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register could not be retrieved for this compilation; the substance of that decision is carried from other sources, but the Library's framing of it is unverified.

The inventory contains nothing on entry, visa screening, border questioning, or airport document inspection as they might affect a trans visitor, including any practice of sex markers on passports being checked against presentation. Nor does it address recognition of foreign legal gender changes, non-binary legal status (which appears only as a survey category), or access to gender-affirming medication for short-term visitors.
